items.stem: Which of the following best describes "critical value"?
options: A statement that there is a difference or relationship, either directional (one-tailed) or non-directional (two-tailed)
The probability threshold (usually p ≤ 0.05) below which the null hypothesis is rejected
How far the findings in a source can be trusted, based on method, sample, measurement, peer review and bias
The value a test statistic must reach (or, for U and T, not exceed) for a result to be significant
items.answer: The value a test statistic must reach (or, for U and T, not exceed) for a result to be significant
items.markingKey: D. "critical value" is the value a test statistic must reach (or, for U and T, not exceed) for a result to be significant.

items.stem: A one-tailed test of the effect of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation gives p = 0.07. The researcher set the significance level at p ≤ 0.05. State whether the result is significant, what the researcher should conclude about the null hypothesis, and which type of error she risks.
items.answer: Not significant (p = 0.07 > 0.05); retain (fail to reject) the null hypothesis; risk of a Type II error (retaining a false null hypothesis - a false negative).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: not significant because p > 0.05. 1 mark: retain H0. 1 mark: a Type II error (retaining a false null hypothesis - a false negative).

items.stem: Explain the difference between effect size and statistical significance.
items.answer: Significance indicates whether a result is unlikely to be due to chance; effect size indicates how large the difference or relationship is.
items.markingKey: Significance indicates whether a result is unlikely to be due to chance; effect size indicates how large the difference or relationship is. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A study tests whether time spent on social media is associated with self-esteem scores in 40 adolescents. Which inferential test is most appropriate?
items.answer: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient
items.markingKey: D. Spearman's rank correlation coefficient: two co-variables; test of association.

items.stem: A correlational study found r = 0.56 between hours of revision and exam percentage. Describe this correlation and explain why it cannot be used to conclude that one variable causes the other.
items.answer: A moderate positive correlation: as hours of revision increases, exam percentage tends to increase. Correlation does not establish causation; a third variable such as age could affect both, or causality could run in the opposite direction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark direction (positive); 1 mark strength (moderate, r = 0.56); 1 mark causality: no IV is manipulated, so third variables (e.g. age) or bidirectional causality cannot be ruled out.

items.stem:
A repeated measures study in Mumbai measured prejudice score before and after a jigsaw classroom unit for 8 participants.
Participant: before | after
P1: 35 | 50
P2: 19 | 22
P3: 23 | 32
P4: 27 | 34
P5: 35 | 48
P6: 22 | 14
P7: 38 | 42
P8: 33 | 35

Calculate the Wilcoxon signed-rank statistic T (rank the absolute differences, then take the smaller of the sums of positive and negative ranks). The critical value of T for n = 8 at p = 0.05 (two-tailed) is 3; T must be equal to or less than this to be significant. State whether the difference is significant.
items.answer: Differences (after - before): [15, 3, 9, 7, 13, -8, 4, 2]; sum of positive ranks = 31, sum of negative ranks = 5; T = 5; not significant at p = 0.05.
items.markingKey: M1 differences after - before: [15, 3, 9, 7, 13, -8, 4, 2]. M1 rank absolute differences (smallest = 1). A1 positive ranks = 31, negative ranks = 5 (total 36 = 8(9)/2). A1 T = 5. R1 T > 3: not significant - retain the null hypothesis.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Statistical significance testing is the best way to evaluate psychological findings."
items.answer: Significance tests are useful but should be combined with effect sizes, confidence intervals, pre-registration and replication.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: objective decision rule; controls for chance; standard across research. Arguments against: arbitrary 0.05 cut-off; ignores effect size and confidence intervals; p-hacking and the replication crisis; significance depends on sample size. Supported judgement: Significance tests are useful but should be combined with effect sizes, confidence intervals, pre-registration and replication.

items.stem:
A researcher in Nairobi investigated the relationship between caffeine intake (mg per day) and self-reported anxiety in 6 participants.
Participant: caffeine intake (mg per day) | self-reported anxiety
P1: 15 | 17
P2: 1 | 26
P3: 39 | 28
P4: 26 | 19
P5: 37 | 22
P6: 21 | 14

Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (rs) using rs = 1 - 6Σd² / (n(n² - 1)), giving your answer to 3 decimal places. The critical value for n = 6 at p = 0.05 (two-tailed) is 0.886. State whether the correlation is significant and what can be concluded.
items.answer: Σd² = 22; rs = 0.371; weak positive correlation; not significant at p = 0.05.
items.markingKey: M1 rank each variable separately (ranks X: [2, 1, 6, 4, 5, 3]; ranks Y: [2, 5, 6, 3, 4, 1]). M1 d² summed: Σd² = 22. A1 rs = 1 - 6(22)/(6(36 - 1)) = 0.371. A1 |rs| < 0.886, so the correlation is not significant; retain the null hypothesis. R1 correlation does not show causation - a third variable could explain the relationship.

items.stem: Which test would be appropriate for a repeated measures design with ordinal data?
items.answer: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
items.markingKey: C. Repeated measures produce related (paired) data.

items.stem: Explain why non-parametric tests are often used in student research.
items.answer: Student studies often have small samples and ordinal data (ratings, scores) that may not be normally distributed; tests using ranks make fewer assumptions.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Student studies often have small samples and ordinal data (ratings, scores) that may not be normally distributed; tests using ranks make fewer assumptions. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "A non-significant result proves that the null hypothesis is true." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It only means there is insufficient evidence to reject H0; the study may lack power (a Type II error is possible).
items.markingKey: It only means there is insufficient evidence to reject H0; the study may lack power (a Type II error is possible). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A researcher finds p = 0.06. Explain what she should conclude and suggest one way she could investigate further.
items.answer: Not significant at 0.05 - retain H0; possible Type II error; replicate with a larger sample (more power), check effect size, reduce extraneous variables.
items.markingKey: Not significant at 0.05 - retain H0; possible Type II error; replicate with a larger sample (more power), check effect size, reduce extraneous variables.

items.stem:
Hana compared the number of words recalled of students who used retrieval practice (group A) and students who re-read their notes (group B), n = 6 in each group.
Group A: 18, 43, 27, 17, 12, 42
Group B: 22, 34, 20, 41, 30, 39

Calculate the Mann-Whitney U statistic, using U = n1n2 + n1(n1 + 1)/2 - R1 for each group and taking the smaller value. The critical value of U for n1 = n2 = 6 at p = 0.05 (two-tailed) is 5; U must be equal to or less than this value to be significant. State your conclusion.
items.answer: RA = 35, RB = 43; UA = 22, UB = 14; U = 14; not significant at p = 0.05.
items.markingKey: M1 rank all 12 scores together (lowest = 1). A1 rank sums RA = 35, RB = 43 (check: RA + RB = 78 = 12(13)/2). M1 UA = 36 + 21 - 35 = 22; UB = 36 - 22 = 14. A1 U = 14. R1 U = 14 > 5, so the difference is not significant - retain the null hypothesis (p > 0.05).

items.stem: Using a mindfulness pilot in Auckland as an example, explain interpreting inferential tests.
items.answer: A school counsellor compared stress ratings of 8 students before and after a mindfulness course; the Wilcoxon test gave T = 4, with a critical value of 3 at p = 0.05. Because T is greater than the critical value, the result is not significant; with only 8 students a real effect may have been missed (possible Type II error)
items.markingKey: Context (A school counsellor compared stress ratings of 8 students before and after a mindfulness course; the Wilcoxon test gave T = 4, with a critical value of 3 at p = 0.05.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: because T is greater than the critical value, the result is not significant; with only 8 students a real effect may have been missed (possible Type II error) – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to interpreting inferential tests.

items.stem: With reference to the six concepts of the course, discuss the claim that statistical significance testing is the best way to evaluate psychological findings.
items.answer: Significance tests are useful but should be combined with effect sizes, confidence intervals, pre-registration and replication.
items.markingKey: For: objective decision rule; controls for chance; standard across research. Against: arbitrary 0.05 cut-off; ignores effect size and confidence intervals; p-hacking and the replication crisis; significance depends on sample size. Supported conclusion: Significance tests are useful but should be combined with effect sizes, confidence intervals, pre-registration and replication. Markbands (15), applied holistically: 13-15 - the response is focused on the command term and the question throughout; knowledge and understanding of the relevant concepts, theories and studies is accurate and detailed; research is clearly explained and explicitly linked to the argument; critical thinking is well developed (methodological, ethical and cultural evaluation, alternative explanations, the six concepts where relevant) and leads to a reasoned conclusion. 10-12 - focused; accurate knowledge; relevant research mostly linked to the question; evaluation present but uneven. 7-9 - partly focused; some accurate knowledge; research described more than used; evaluation limited or generic. 4-6 - limited focus; knowledge partly accurate; research only named or poorly linked; little evaluation. 1-3 - very limited relevant knowledge, no evaluation. 0 - does not reach band 1.

items.stem: A source reports rs = -0.62 between hours of gaming and sleep duration. This shows:
items.answer: A moderate-to-strong negative correlation
items.markingKey: A moderate-to-strong negative correlation. Correlation does not establish causation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a qualitative source and a quantitative source.
items.answer: A quantitative source presents numerical data that can be summarised and tested statistically; a qualitative source presents words or observations interpreted for meaning and themes.
items.markingKey: A quantitative source presents numerical data that can be summarised and tested statistically; a qualitative source presents words or observations interpreted for meaning and themes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Sana writes: "The condition with the higher mean must be better." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Without considering spread, sample size and an inferential test, a higher mean may reflect chance.
items.markingKey: Without considering spread, sample size and an inferential test, a higher mean may reflect chance. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Zara recorded the following frequencies: agree = 32; neutral = 6; disagree = 44. Calculate the percentage of the total that was "agree" (to 1 decimal place) and identify the modal category.
items.answer: 39.0%; modal category: disagree

items.stem:
The source below is taken from a a focus group with retired teachers in Kyoto about using smartphones.

"My grandson set it up and now I video-call him every Sunday." / "There are so many buttons that I worry I will break something." / "I use it to read the news, but my eyes get tired."

Outline two themes that are suggested by this qualitative source.
items.answer: Possible themes: technology supports family relationships; fear of making mistakes; physical difficulties with screens.
items.markingKey: 2 x (1 mark theme identified + 1 mark supported by a quotation from the source). Indicative: technology supports family relationships; fear of making mistakes; physical difficulties with screens.

items.stem:
Noah tested the hypothesis that self-rated anxiety (1-10) before giving a speech would be higher before speaking to an audience of 50 than before speaking to a group of 3.

Condition A (before speaking to an audience of 50): 10, 9, 7, 1, 7, 9, 1, 8
Condition B (before speaking to a group of 3): 9, 8, 5, 1, 7, 6, 1, 6

Calculate the mean and sample standard deviation for each condition (to 2 decimal places). State whether the descriptive statistics are in the direction predicted by the hypothesis and compare the spread of the two conditions.
items.answer: Mean A = 6.50, SD A = 3.55; mean B = 5.38, SD B = 2.97. The means are in the predicted direction. Condition A has the larger SD, so its scores are more spread out (less consistent). Descriptive statistics alone cannot show that the difference is significant; an inferential test is needed.
items.markingKey: A1 means: A = 52/8 = 6.50, B = 43/8 = 5.38. A1 SD A = 3.55. A1 SD B = 2.97. R1 direction: supports the hypothesis. R1 spread: condition A is more variable. R1 recognises that significance requires an inferential test.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A measure of how spread out scores are around the mean"?
items.answer: standard deviation
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of standard deviation.

items.stem: Explain how combining quantitative and qualitative sources can strengthen a conclusion.
items.answer: Quantitative data show the size and pattern of an effect in a larger sample; qualitative data explain why it occurs and how participants experience it; agreement between them (method triangulation) increases credibility.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Quantitative data show the size and pattern of an effect in a larger sample; qualitative data explain why it occurs and how participants experience it; agreement between them (method triangulation) increases credibility. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Qualitative sources are less scientific and cannot be evaluated." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Qualitative sources are evaluated with criteria such as credibility, transferability, reflexivity and triangulation.
items.markingKey: Qualitative sources are evaluated with criteria such as credibility, transferability, reflexivity and triangulation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The raw data below show self-rated anxiety (1-10) before giving a speech for 9 participants in a class practical: 4, 5, 6, 4, 3, 3, 5, 2, 3. Calculate the mean (to 2 decimal places) and the median, and explain which is the more appropriate measure of central tendency for these data.
items.answer: Mean = 3.89; median = 4; more appropriate: the mean, because there are no extreme scores and the data are at least interval-like, so the mean uses every value.
items.markingKey: A1 mean = 35/9 = 3.89. A1 median = 4 (ordered: 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6). R2: the mean, because there are no extreme scores and the data are at least interval-like, so the mean uses every value.

items.stem: With reference to the six concepts of the course, discuss the claim that quantitative sources are more useful than qualitative sources for answering research questions.
items.answer: Usefulness depends on the research question; combining both types usually gives the strongest conclusion.
items.markingKey: For: statistical testing and generalisation; large samples; replicability. Against: qualitative sources explain meaning and context; more valid for experiences; mixed methods are often strongest. Supported conclusion: Usefulness depends on the research question; combining both types usually gives the strongest conclusion. Markbands (scaled to the marks available): top band - focused on the command term, accurate and detailed knowledge, research explicitly used as evidence, well-developed evaluation (methods, ethics, culture, alternative explanations) and a reasoned conclusion; middle band - mostly focused, relevant research partly linked, evaluation uneven; lower band - descriptive, research named but not used, little evaluation.

items.stem: In the final, highest-mark Paper 3 question, candidates are expected to:
items.answer: Synthesise evidence from all the sources and their own knowledge into a reasoned conclusion
items.markingKey: Synthesise evidence from all the sources and their own knowledge into a reasoned conclusion. Synthesis and evaluation earn the top markband.

items.stem: Explain why time management is important in Paper 3.
items.answer: The final synthesis question carries half the marks; spending too long on short questions leaves too little time to integrate all sources and own knowledge.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The final synthesis question carries half the marks; spending too long on short questions leaves too little time to integrate all sources and own knowledge. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between describing a source and evaluating a source.
items.answer: Describing a source reports what it says; evaluating a source judges how trustworthy and useful its evidence is, considering method, sample and bias.
items.markingKey: Describing a source reports what it says; evaluating a source judges how trustworthy and useful its evidence is, considering method, sample and bias. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A source gives no information about how participants were recruited. Explain why this matters for evaluating it.
items.answer: Without knowing the sampling method we cannot judge representativeness or self-selection bias, so it is unclear how far the findings generalise.
items.markingKey: Without knowing the sampling method we cannot judge representativeness or self-selection bias, so it is unclear how far the findings generalise.

items.stem: "A longer answer always gets more marks." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Marks depend on meeting the command term with relevant, source-based evidence; padding or irrelevant description does not earn marks.
items.markingKey: Marks depend on meeting the command term with relevant, source-based evidence; padding or irrelevant description does not earn marks. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to running out of time, explain how it illustrates time management in Paper 3.
items.answer: A candidate wrote two pages for the 3-mark question and had 10 minutes left for the 15-mark synthesis question, which he answered using only Source A. Over-writing early questions reduced time for the highest-mark question, and using one source limits marks to lower bands
items.markingKey: Context (A candidate wrote two pages for the 3-mark question and had 10 minutes left for the 15-mark synthesis question, which he answered using only Source A.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: over-writing early questions reduced time for the highest-mark question, and using one source limits marks to lower bands – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to time management in Paper 3.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Qualitative sources provide stronger evidence than quantitative sources in Paper 3."
items.answer: Neither is stronger in general; the best answers weigh each source's credibility and combine them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rich insight into experiences; participants' own meanings; can explain quantitative patterns. Arguments against: small samples limit transferability; researcher interpretation and bias; cannot measure effect size. Supported judgement: Neither is stronger in general; the best answers weigh each source's credibility and combine them.

items.stem: Source A (survey of 2,000 students in five countries) finds a small negative correlation between phone use and grades; Source B (experiment, n = 60) finds that phones on the desk reduce attention; Source C (interviews with 10 students) reports that phones help with group study. Discuss what these sources suggest about the effect of phones on learning.
items.answer: Source A: large, cross-cultural but correlational, small effect; Source B: causal but small sample and artificial; Source C: rich but small sample, shows benefits; own knowledge: Ward et al. (2017), Sana et al. (2013); conclusion: phones can impair attention when present/used for distraction, but effects depend on use; evidence quality varies.
items.markingKey: Source A: large, cross-cultural but correlational, small effect; Source B: causal but small sample and artificial; Source C: rich but small sample, shows benefits; own knowledge: Ward et al. (2017), Sana et al. (2013); conclusion: phones can impair attention when present/used for distraction, but effects depend on use; evidence quality varies.

items.stem: With 1 hour 45 minutes for 30 marks in Paper 3, roughly how long should a candidate spend on a 6-mark question?
items.answer: About 20 minutes
items.markingKey: A. 105 minutes / 30 marks = 3.5 minutes per mark; 6 x 3.5 = 21 minutes.

items.stem: Jonas writes: "In Paper 3 you should ignore your own knowledge and only use the sources." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The sources are the main evidence, but relevant own knowledge (theories, studies, concepts) is needed to reach the top markbands in the synthesis question.
items.markingKey: The sources are the main evidence, but relevant own knowledge (theories, studies, concepts) is needed to reach the top markbands in the synthesis question. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how a candidate can evaluate a source in a Paper 3 answer.
items.answer: Comment on the method (design, controls), sample (size, representativeness, culture), measurement (reliability, validity), credibility (peer review, funding, triangulation) and how these affect the conclusions that can be drawn.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Comment on the method (design, controls), sample (size, representativeness, culture), measurement (reliability, validity), credibility (peer review, funding, triangulation) and how these affect the conclusions that can be drawn. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Maya is sitting a mock Paper 3 lasting 90 minutes for 35 marks. Calculate the time per mark and how long Maya should spend on a 4-mark question. Suggest how Maya should use any time saved on short questions.
items.answer: 90/35 = 2.6 min per mark; 4 marks x 2.6 = 10 minutes. Use saved time to plan and synthesise the highest-mark question.
items.markingKey: A1 2.6 min per mark (accept 2.57). A1 about 10 minutes. R1 sensible use of time (planning/synthesis/checking).

items.stem: Chloé is sitting an end-of-unit paper lasting 90 minutes for 35 marks. Calculate the time per mark and how long Chloé should spend on a 8-mark question. Suggest how Chloé should use any time saved on short questions.
items.answer: 90/35 = 2.6 min per mark; 8 marks x 2.6 = 21 minutes. Use saved time to plan and synthesise the highest-mark question.
items.markingKey: A1 2.6 min per mark (accept 2.57). A1 about 21 minutes. R1 sensible use of time (planning/synthesis/checking).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Correlational sources are of limited use when answering Paper 3 questions."
items.answer: Correlational sources are useful when their limits are acknowledged and they are combined with experimental and qualitative evidence.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: cannot show causation; third variables; often self-report. Arguments against: large samples and real-world data; show patterns that experiments cannot ethically test; can be combined with experimental sources. Supported judgement: Correlational sources are useful when their limits are acknowledged and they are combined with experimental and qualitative evidence.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "alternative hypothesis (H1)".
items.answer: A statement that there is a difference or relationship, either directional (one-tailed) or non-directional (two-tailed)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a statement that there is a difference or relationship, either directional (one-tailed) or non-directional (two-tailed). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "command term "evaluate""?
options: Make an appraisal by weighing up strengths and limitations
Offer a considered and balanced review that includes a range of arguments, factors or hypotheses
A test such as Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon or Spearman that uses ranks and does not assume normally distributed interval data
A source presenting non-numerical data, such as interview extracts, observation notes or themes
items.answer: Make an appraisal by weighing up strengths and limitations
items.markingKey: A. "command term "evaluate"" is make an appraisal by weighing up strengths and limitations.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "credibility of a source"?
options: A detailed account of context and participants that allows readers to judge transferability
A test such as Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon or Spearman that uses ranks and does not assume normally distributed interval data
How far the findings in a source can be trusted, based on method, sample, measurement, peer review and bias
An exam question that asks candidates to use given sources, together with their own knowledge, to answer it
items.answer: How far the findings in a source can be trusted, based on method, sample, measurement, peer review and bias
items.markingKey: C. "credibility of a source" is how far the findings in a source can be trusted, based on method, sample, measurement, peer review and bias.

items.stem: Maya writes: "A non-significant result proves that the null hypothesis is true." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It only means there is insufficient evidence to reject H0; the study may lack power (a Type II error is possible).
items.markingKey: It only means there is insufficient evidence to reject H0; the study may lack power (a Type II error is possible). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between describing a source and evaluating a source.
items.answer: Describing a source reports what it says; evaluating a source judges how trustworthy and useful its evidence is, considering method, sample and bias.
items.markingKey: Describing a source reports what it says; evaluating a source judges how trustworthy and useful its evidence is, considering method, sample and bias. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why it is important to consider the spread of data as well as the mean.
items.answer: Two conditions can have similar means but very different variability; a high SD suggests individual differences or extraneous variables and makes a difference in means less reliable.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Two conditions can have similar means but very different variability; a high SD suggests individual differences or extraneous variables and makes a difference in means less reliable. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why a statistically significant result is not necessarily an important result.
items.answer: Significance depends on sample size; with very large samples tiny effects become significant (e.g. Orben and Przybylski, 2019), so effect size and practical importance must also be considered.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Significance depends on sample size; with very large samples tiny effects become significant (e.g. Orben and Przybylski, 2019), so effect size and practical importance must also be considered. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between using a source and using own knowledge.
items.answer: Using a source means citing its data or quotations as evidence; own knowledge means adding relevant theory or research not given in the sources to support or challenge them.
items.markingKey: Using a source means citing its data or quotations as evidence; own knowledge means adding relevant theory or research not given in the sources to support or challenge them. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between transferability and generalisability.
items.answer: Generalisability is the extent to which quantitative findings from a sample apply to a population; transferability is the extent to which qualitative findings apply to other contexts, judged by the reader using thick description.
items.markingKey: Generalisability is the extent to which quantitative findings from a sample apply to a population; transferability is the extent to which qualitative findings apply to other contexts, judged by the reader using thick description. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Chloé reports a correlation coefficient of -0.21 between caffeine intake (mg per day) and self-reported anxiety. Interpret the direction and strength of this relationship, and suggest one third variable that could explain it.
items.answer: A weak negative correlation: as caffeine intake (mg per day) increases, self-reported anxiety tends to decrease. Correlation does not establish causation; a third variable such as stress levels could affect both, or causality could run in the opposite direction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark direction (negative); 1 mark strength (weak, r = -0.21); 1 mark causality: no IV is manipulated, so third variables (e.g. stress levels) or bidirectional causality cannot be ruled out.

items.stem: Using running out of time as an example, explain time management in Paper 3.
items.answer: A candidate wrote two pages for the 3-mark question and had 10 minutes left for the 15-mark synthesis question, which he answered using only Source A. Over-writing early questions reduced time for the highest-mark question, and using one source limits marks to lower bands
items.markingKey: Context (A candidate wrote two pages for the 3-mark question and had 10 minutes left for the 15-mark synthesis question, which he answered using only Source A.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: over-writing early questions reduced time for the highest-mark question, and using one source limits marks to lower bands – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to time management in Paper 3.

items.stem: With reference to mixed-methods evaluation in Lima, explain how it illustrates combining quantitative and qualitative sources.
items.answer: Source C: a reading programme raised mean test scores by 8 points; interviews with teachers said pupils "finally enjoyed books". The numerical gain is supported by qualitative evidence about motivation, increasing credibility through method triangulation
items.markingKey: Context (Source C: a reading programme raised mean test scores by 8 points; interviews with teachers said pupils "finally enjoyed books".) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the numerical gain is supported by qualitative evidence about motivation, increasing credibility through method triangulation – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to combining quantitative and qualitative sources.

items.stem: Using a replication of the testing effect in Lyon as an example, explain interpreting Mann-Whitney U.
items.answer: Students who used retrieval practice recalled more than students who re-read; a Mann-Whitney test gave U = 9 with n = 10 per group (critical value 23). U = 9 is below the critical value of 23, so the difference is significant at p = 0.05 and H0 is rejected
items.markingKey: Context (Students who used retrieval practice recalled more than students who re-read; a Mann-Whitney test gave U = 9 with n = 10 per group (critical value 23).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: U = 9 is below the critical value of 23, so the difference is significant at p = 0.05 and H0 is rejected – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to interpreting Mann-Whitney U.

items.stem: A source shows that 30 participants in Cairo were recruited from one gym. Explain one implication for the conclusions a candidate can draw.
items.answer: Opportunity/self-selected sample from one gym - likely fitter and more health-motivated than the population, so findings may not generalise; conclusions should be limited to similar groups.
items.markingKey: Opportunity/self-selected sample from one gym - likely fitter and more health-motivated than the population, so findings may not generalise; conclusions should be limited to similar groups.

items.stem:
Sofia and Jonas used time sampling to code students' behaviour in a lesson every 30 seconds (N = on-task, F = off-task, D = disruptive).
Sofia: D F D N D N D D F N N F D F N N D D D F
Jonas: F F N N D F D D F N N F D D N N D D D F

Calculate the percentage agreement between the two observers and explain whether inter-rater reliability is acceptable.
items.answer: 16/20 intervals agree = 80.0%; acceptable (the usual benchmark is 80%).
items.markingKey: M1 agreements counted: 16 of 20. A1 16/20 x 100 = 80.0%. R1 ≥ 80%, so reliability is acceptable.

items.stem: A two-tailed test of the effect of spaced practice on recall gives p = 0.07. The researcher set the significance level at p ≤ 0.05. State whether the result is significant, what the researcher should conclude about the null hypothesis, and which type of error she risks.
items.answer: Not significant (p = 0.07 > 0.05); retain (fail to reject) the null hypothesis; risk of a Type II error (retaining a false null hypothesis - a false negative).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: not significant because p > 0.05. 1 mark: retain H0. 1 mark: a Type II error (retaining a false null hypothesis - a false negative).

items.stem: A Paper 3 source states: "Our app reduced anxiety by 30% in four weeks" and is published on the app developer's website. To what extent should this source be trusted?
items.answer: Limited trust: conflict of interest; not peer reviewed; unclear design (control group? random allocation?), sample and measure; percentage may hide small absolute change; could be supported if independent RCTs replicate; judgement: low credibility until verified.
items.markingKey: Limited trust: conflict of interest; not peer reviewed; unclear design (control group? random allocation?), sample and measure; percentage may hide small absolute change; could be supported if independent RCTs replicate; judgement: low credibility until verified.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Quantitative sources are more useful than qualitative sources for answering research questions."
items.answer: Usefulness depends on the research question; combining both types usually gives the strongest conclusion.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: statistical testing and generalisation; large samples; replicability. Arguments against: qualitative sources explain meaning and context; more valid for experiences; mixed methods are often strongest. Supported judgement: Usefulness depends on the research question; combining both types usually gives the strongest conclusion. Markbands (8 marks): Markbands (15), applied holistically: 13-15 - the response is focused on the command term and the question throughout; knowledge and understanding of the relevant concepts, theories and studies is accurate and detailed; research is clearly explained and explicitly linked to the argument; critical thinking is well developed (methodological, ethical and cultural evaluation, alternative explanations, the six concepts where relevant) and leads to a reasoned conclusion. 10-12 - focused; accurate knowledge; relevant research mostly linked to the question; evaluation present but uneven. 7-9 - partly focused; some accurate knowledge; research described more than used; evaluation limited or generic. 4-6 - limited focus; knowledge partly accurate; research only named or poorly linked; little evaluation. 1-3 - very limited relevant knowledge, no evaluation. 0 - does not reach band 1.

items.stem: "Statistical significance testing is the best way to evaluate psychological findings." Discuss.
items.answer: Significance tests are useful but should be combined with effect sizes, confidence intervals, pre-registration and replication.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: objective decision rule; controls for chance; standard across research. Arguments against: arbitrary 0.05 cut-off; ignores effect size and confidence intervals; p-hacking and the replication crisis; significance depends on sample size. Supported judgement: Significance tests are useful but should be combined with effect sizes, confidence intervals, pre-registration and replication. items.stem: Using two relevant studies, discuss the claim that qualitative sources provide stronger evidence than quantitative sources in Paper 3.
items.answer: Neither is stronger in general; the best answers weigh each source's credibility and combine them.
items.markingKey: For: rich insight into experiences; participants' own meanings; can explain quantitative patterns. Against: small samples limit transferability; researcher interpretation and bias; cannot measure effect size. Supported conclusion: Neither is stronger in general; the best answers weigh each source's credibility and combine them. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Retaining a null hypothesis that is actually false (a false negative)"?
items.answer: Type II error
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of Type II error.

items.stem: Define the term "command term "discuss"".
items.answer: Offer a considered and balanced review that includes a range of arguments, factors or hypotheses
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: offer a considered and balanced review that includes a range of arguments, factors or hypotheses. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "thick description".
items.answer: A detailed account of context and participants that allows readers to judge transferability
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a detailed account of context and participants that allows readers to judge transferability. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Ingrid writes: "p = 0.001 shows a much larger effect than p = 0.04." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: p-values depend on sample size as well as effect size; a large sample can give a tiny p for a small effect.
items.markingKey: p-values depend on sample size as well as effect size; a large sample can give a tiny p for a small effect. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "A longer answer always gets more marks." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Marks depend on meeting the command term with relevant, source-based evidence; padding or irrelevant description does not earn marks.
items.markingKey: Marks depend on meeting the command term with relevant, source-based evidence; padding or irrelevant description does not earn marks. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between transferability and generalisability.
items.answer: Generalisability is the extent to which quantitative findings from a sample apply to a population; transferability is the extent to which qualitative findings apply to other contexts, judged by the reader using thick description.
items.markingKey: Generalisability is the extent to which quantitative findings from a sample apply to a population; transferability is the extent to which qualitative findings apply to other contexts, judged by the reader using thick description. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A correlational study found r = 0.05 between daily screen time (hours) and sustained-attention score. Describe this correlation and explain why it cannot be used to conclude that one variable causes the other.
items.answer: A negligible (close to zero) positive correlation: as daily screen time (hours) increases, sustained-attention score tends to increase. Correlation does not establish causation; a third variable such as stress levels could affect both, or causality could run in the opposite direction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark direction (positive); 1 mark strength (negligible (close to zero), r = 0.05); 1 mark causality: no IV is manipulated, so third variables (e.g. stress levels) or bidirectional causality cannot be ruled out.

items.stem: "In Paper 3 you should ignore your own knowledge and only use the sources." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The sources are the main evidence, but relevant own knowledge (theories, studies, concepts) is needed to reach the top markbands in the synthesis question.
items.markingKey: The sources are the main evidence, but relevant own knowledge (theories, studies, concepts) is needed to reach the top markbands in the synthesis question. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why a correlation in a source cannot establish cause and effect.
items.answer: Neither variable is manipulated; the relationship may be bidirectional or caused by a third variable.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Neither variable is manipulated; the relationship may be bidirectional or caused by a third variable. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student wants to test whether boys and girls differ in their ratings (1-10) of fear of missing out. Identify an appropriate inferential test and justify your choice.
items.answer: Mann-Whitney U: two independent groups (boys/girls), test of difference, ordinal rating data.
items.markingKey: Mann-Whitney U: two independent groups (boys/girls), test of difference, ordinal rating data.

items.stem: With reference to a well-planned synthesis answer, explain how it illustrates Paper 3 synthesis skills.
items.answer: A candidate planned for 5 minutes, then wrote paragraphs each combining one source with a study from her own knowledge, evaluated the sources' samples and ended with a qualified conclusion. Integrating sources with own knowledge, evaluating them and reaching a reasoned judgement meets the top markband descriptors
items.markingKey: Context (A candidate planned for 5 minutes, then wrote paragraphs each combining one source with a study from her own knowledge, evaluated the sources' samples and ended with a qualified conclusion.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: integrating sources with own knowledge, evaluating them and reaching a reasoned judgement meets the top markband descriptors – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to Paper 3 synthesis skills.

items.stem: A Paper 3 source reports that 64% of 50 surveyed students "agree" that social media harms their concentration. Explain two limitations of this source.
items.answer: Self-report/social desirability; small, possibly unrepresentative sample; leading wording of the item; correlational opinion data cannot show cause; percentages hide strength of agreement.
items.markingKey: Self-report/social desirability; small, possibly unrepresentative sample; leading wording of the item; correlational opinion data cannot show cause; percentages hide strength of agreement.

items.stem:
Elena compared the number of times a confederate was helped of participants tested alone (group A) and participants tested in a group of four (group B), n = 6 in each group.
Group A: 9, 15, 49, 20, 55, 53
Group B: 33, 39, 48, 24, 34, 45

Calculate the Mann-Whitney U statistic, using U = n1n2 + n1(n1 + 1)/2 - R1 for each group and taking the smaller value. The critical value of U for n1 = n2 = 6 at p = 0.05 (two-tailed) is 5; U must be equal to or less than this value to be significant. State your conclusion.
items.answer: RA = 39, RB = 39; UA = 18, UB = 18; U = 18; not significant at p = 0.05.
items.markingKey: M1 rank all 12 scores together (lowest = 1). A1 rank sums RA = 39, RB = 39 (check: RA + RB = 78 = 12(13)/2). M1 UA = 36 + 21 - 39 = 18; UB = 36 - 18 = 18. A1 U = 18. R1 U = 18 > 5, so the difference is not significant - retain the null hypothesis (p > 0.05).

items.stem: Mateo is sitting a timed practice paper lasting 105 minutes for 30 marks. Calculate the time per mark and how long Mateo should spend on a 5-mark question. Suggest how Mateo should use any time saved on short questions.
items.answer: 105/30 = 3.5 min per mark; 5 marks x 3.5 = 18 minutes. Use saved time to plan and synthesise the highest-mark question.
items.markingKey: A1 3.5 min per mark (accept 3.50). A1 about 18 minutes. R1 sensible use of time (planning/synthesis/checking).

items.stem:
Kwame and Priya used time sampling to code interactions in a school canteen every 30 seconds (P = prosocial, N = neutral, A = aggressive).
Kwame: N P N P P A N P N A N N P P P P N A N P
Priya: N P N P P A N P A P N N P N P P N A N N

Calculate the percentage agreement between the two observers and explain whether inter-rater reliability is acceptable.
items.answer: 16/20 intervals agree = 80.0%; acceptable (the usual benchmark is 80%).
items.markingKey: M1 agreements counted: 16 of 20. A1 16/20 x 100 = 80.0%. R1 ≥ 80%, so reliability is acceptable.

items.stem:
A repeated measures study in Singapore measured self-efficacy score before and after watching a peer model for 6 participants.
Participant: before | after
P1: 22 | 30
P2: 19 | 26
P3: 28 | 22
P4: 22 | 25
P5: 40 | 41
P6: 39 | 50

Calculate the Wilcoxon signed-rank statistic T (rank the absolute differences, then take the smaller of the sums of positive and negative ranks). The critical value of T for n = 6 at p = 0.05 (two-tailed) is 0; T must be equal to or less than this to be significant. State whether the difference is significant.
items.answer: Differences (after - before): [8, 7, -6, 3, 1, 11]; sum of positive ranks = 18, sum of negative ranks = 3; T = 3; not significant at p = 0.05.
items.markingKey: M1 differences after - before: [8, 7, -6, 3, 1, 11]. M1 rank absolute differences (smallest = 1). A1 positive ranks = 18, negative ranks = 3 (total 21 = 6(7)/2). A1 T = 3. R1 T > 0: not significant - retain the null hypothesis.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Qualitative sources provide stronger evidence than quantitative sources in Paper 3."
items.answer: Neither is stronger in general; the best answers weigh each source's credibility and combine them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rich insight into experiences; participants' own meanings; can explain quantitative patterns. Arguments against: small samples limit transferability; researcher interpretation and bias; cannot measure effect size. Supported judgement: Neither is stronger in general; the best answers weigh each source's credibility and combine them.

items.stem:
Source B reports data from a a focus group with retired teachers in Kyoto about using smartphones.

"My grandson set it up and now I video-call him every Sunday." / "There are so many buttons that I worry I will break something." / "I use it to read the news, but my eyes get tired."

To what extent can the conclusions drawn from this source be applied beyond the participants? Refer to the source in your answer.
items.answer: Transferability is limited: small, specific sample (a focus group with retired teachers in Kyoto); context-specific experiences; but thick description of themes (technology supports family relationships; fear of making mistakes; physical difficulties with screens) allows readers to judge similarity to other contexts; triangulation with other sources would increase confidence.
items.markingKey: 5-6: balanced judgement on transferability explicitly linked to features of the source (sample size and selection, setting, method, thick description, researcher bias); 3-4: relevant points, partly generic; 1-2: limited or descriptive. Themes in the source: technology supports family relationships; fear of making mistakes; physical difficulties with screens.

items.stem:
A researcher in Kuala Lumpur investigated the relationship between years of experience as a taxi driver and posterior hippocampal volume rank in 7 participants.
Participant: years of experience as a taxi driver | posterior hippocampal volume rank
P1: 11 | 14
P2: 24 | 25
P3: 27 | 32
P4: 29 | 20
P5: 26 | 23
P6: 28 | 17
P7: 15 | 28

Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (rs) using rs = 1 - 6Σd² / (n(n² - 1)), giving your answer to 3 decimal places. The critical value for n = 7 at p = 0.05 (two-tailed) is 0.786. State whether the correlation is significant and what can be concluded.
items.answer: Σd² = 56; rs = 0.000; weak no correlation; not significant at p = 0.05.
items.markingKey: M1 rank each variable separately (ranks X: [1, 3, 5, 7, 4, 6, 2]; ranks Y: [1, 5, 7, 3, 4, 2, 6]). M1 d² summed: Σd² = 56. A1 rs = 1 - 6(56)/(7(49 - 1)) = 0.000. A1 |rs| < 0.786, so the correlation is not significant; retain the null hypothesis. R1 correlation does not show causation - a third variable could explain the relationship.

items.stem: "The skills tested in Paper 3 are the most important skills for a psychologist." Evaluate this claim with reference to research.
items.answer: Source evaluation and synthesis are central, but practical and ethical skills are equally important.
items.markingKey: For: evaluating evidence and synthesising sources is core to research; transferable critical thinking. Against: psychologists also need practical research and ethical skills; timed conditions differ from real research; content knowledge is also essential. Supported conclusion: Source evaluation and synthesis are central, but practical and ethical skills are equally important.
